problem.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problem.prompt: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. Return the answer in any order. The algorithm must be better than O(N log N), where N is the array length.

spark.summary: Find the k most frequent integers without sorting all elements. Count occurrences, group values by frequency, and scan buckets from highest to lowest.
spark.keyTakeaway: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, frequency cannot exceed the input length. Use that bounded range as bucket indices to select the top k in O(N) expected time and O(N) auxiliary space.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Given an integer array `nums` (`1 <= nums.length <= 100,000`, `-10,000 <= nums[i] <= 10,000`) and `1 <= k <= U` (where `U` is unique elements), we must return the `k` most frequent elements in strictly better than `O(N log N)` time.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Frequency Map -> Frequency Buckets -> Descending Scan (nums (len N) -> Freq Map (U) -> Buckets [1..N] -> Result (len k)); Hash Map -> Lazy Frequency Buckets -> Early-Return Scan (Input nums[0..N-1] -> Map<val, count> -> buckets[1..N] -> Top-K Collector (stop at k)).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choosing the wrong selection strategy degrades throughput as `N` and `k` grow: 1. Execute three linear passes (`O(N)` expected time, `O(N)` auxiliary space) without mutating `nums`: 1.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Top-K heavy-hitter selection is a core building block in streaming and analytics: **Real-Time Trending Topics & Hashtags**: Combines local node Top-K summaries or Count-Min Sketch + min-heap.

learningJourney.title: Complexity gap: O(N log N) sort vs. O(N log k) heap vs. O(N) buckets

explanation.foundation: Choosing the wrong selection strategy degrades throughput as `N` and `k` grow:
explanation.core:
1. **Full Sort (`O(U log U)`)**: Violates the `< O(N log N)` constraint when `U ≈ N` (`100,000` unique values).
2. **Min-Heap of Size `k` (`O(N + U log k)`)**: Still pays `O(U log k)` comparisons when `k` is large (`k ≈ N/2`), and still requires the `O(U)` frequency map.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Top K Frequent Elements without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, frequency cannot exceed the input length. Use that bounded range as bucket indices to select the top k in O(N) expected time and O(N) auxiliary space.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: Common pitfalls: value-indexed buckets, shared fill([]), and boundary ties

explanation.foundation: Three common bugs break naive implementations:
explanation.core:
- **Indexing buckets by `nums[i]`**: Fails on negative integers (`-10,000 <= nums[i]`).
- **`new Array(N + 1).fill([])`**: Shares the exact same array reference across all `N + 1` slots!
- **Pushing an entire bucket without checking `result.length === k`**: Can return more than `k` elements.

learningJourney.title: Optimal O(N) solution: Frequency Hash Map + Bounded Bucket Array

explanation.foundation: Execute three linear passes (`O(N)` expected time, `O(N)` auxiliary space) without mutating `nums`:
explanation.core:
1. **Count (`O(N)`)**: Build `Map<number, number>` mapping each distinct integer to its frequency.
2. **Group by Frequency (`O(U)`)**: Allocate `buckets` of length `nums.length + 1` (`undefined` slots, lazily initialized) and push `num` into `buckets[count]`.
3. **Collect Top-K (`O(N)`)**: Scan `freq` from `N` down to `1`, pushing elements one by one and returning immediately once `result.length === k`.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does `new Array(nums.length + 1).fill([])` introduce a bug when building frequency buckets in JavaScript/TypeScript?

options.text: fill([]) places the exact same array reference in every slot, so pushing to buckets[count] mutates all buckets at once
options.feedback: Correct: lazily initialize `(buckets[count] ??= []).push(num)` so each populated frequency has its own array.

options.text: JavaScript arrays cannot hold negative numbers
options.feedback: Arrays can hold any number, including negatives.
It allocates one shared array, causing reference aliasing rather than O(N^2) memory.

prerequisites.title: Database Indexing: B-Trees vs LSM-Trees
prerequisites.summary: B-Trees organize sorted keys into fixed-size mutable pages optimized for fast, predictable point and range reads, whereas LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted runs to disk for high write throughput.

prerequisites.title: Distributed & Application Caching
prerequisites.summary: Caching keeps a reusable copy of data so an application can avoid repeating a database query, calculation, or network call. It can make responses faster and reduce database load. The trade-off: the copy may be out of date.

_nextProblem.title: Scaling the Transactional Outbox with CDC
_nextProblem.prompt: Your payment ledger writes 15,000 transactions/sec into PostgreSQL 16, inserting one row into `outbox_events` per transaction. Eight relay workers poll `outbox_events` every 50ms using `SELECT ... WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY id LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and then `UPDATE status = 'SENT'` (or `DELETE`). Within 4 hours of peak load, `outbox_events` bloats from 200 MB to 48 GB despite holding only 50,000 pending rows, autovacuum lags behind due to long-running analytics queries, polling p99 jumps from 8ms to 1,400ms, and Kafka lag exceeds 400,000 events. Redesign the outbox ingestion and relay pipeline to sustain 20,000+ events/sec with < 50ms end-to-end publish latency and zero table bloat.
